e.etymology: From the Italian surname De Luca, of Luca, the Italian form of Luke. Its use as a first name has grown with the popularity of Luca.
A recent American coinage that extends Kai with a -zyn ending, in the pattern of Kaison and Jaxon. It also echoes kaizen, the Japanese word for continuous improvement.
An English surname of Norman origin, a variant of Lovell, from Old French lou, wolf, with a diminutive ending. It has been used as a first name in the US since the 1800s.

assoc.t: Lowell, Massachusetts, historic textile mill city

e.etymology: A spelling of Jordan, the river of the Bible, from Hebrew Yarden, from a verb meaning to descend. Crusaders who carried its water home for baptisms made it a given name in Europe.
The Spanish pet form of Rosa, rose, made with the diminutive ending -ita.
namesakes: Rosita (the bilingual turquoise monster on Sesame Street)
Rosita Espinosa (character in The Walking Dead)

e.etymology: A phonetic spelling of Jacqueline, the French feminine of Jacques, a form of Jacob and James. This spelling is especially common in Latin American families.
The Spanish and Portuguese form of Hannibal, from Punic words meaning grace of the god Baal. It recalls the Carthaginian general who crossed the Alps to fight Rome.

e.meaning: rye clearing; also from an Irish surname
e.etymology: A respelling of Riley with the -leigh ending. Riley is an English surname meaning rye clearing and also the Irish surname Reilly, from O Raghallaigh.

e.meaning: God is my judge (Hebrew); near, within reach (Arabic)
e.etymology: Used as a feminine name in the Daniel family, from Hebrew for God is my judge, and as a spelling of Arabic Dania, close or within reach. In Russian, Danya is a boy's pet form of Daniil.
A spelling of Brooklyn that reads as Brooke plus Lynn. Brooklyn, the New York City borough, takes its name from the Dutch town of Breukelen.
A variant of Jaslyn and Jazlyn, modern blends of Jasmine with a -lyn or -lene ending. It jumped in 2008 after Jaslene Gonzalez won America's Next Top Model.
From Greek pan, all, and doron, gift. In myth Pandora was the first woman, whose opened jar released every evil into the world and kept only hope inside.

assoc.t: Pandora, the alien moon in the Avatar films

e.note: Opening Pandora's box is a common phrase for starting trouble that cannot be undone.

e.etymology: An American spelling of French Coralie, from the word for coral. It is also read as a blend of Cora and Lee.
From Hebrew Gamliel, God is my reward. Gamaliel was a revered first-century rabbi who, in the New Testament, taught the apostle Paul. It was also President Warren G. Harding's middle name.
A short form of Alexander used as a full name in the Netherlands, Norway and Estonia. Alexander is from Greek alexein, to defend, and aner, man.
A surname used as a first name alongside Landon and Landry. Lander is also the Basque form of Leander, a Greek name meaning lion man.

e.meaning: mythical firebird reborn from its ashes
e.etymology: A common respelling of Phoenix, the mythical bird that rises renewed from its own ashes, from Greek phoinix. Phoenix is also the capital of Arizona.
e.note: The standard spelling is Phoenix; with the e before the o, this one is often read as a misspelling.

e.etymology: A one-word form of the Spanish double name Ana Sofia: Ana from Hebrew Hannah, grace, and Sofia from Greek sophia, wisdom.
A form of Ariana or Ariane seen mainly in Latin American families. Those names go back to Greek Ariadne.
The Italian masculine of Amelia, a name from the Germanic element amal, vigor, that has long been mixed up with the Roman family name Aemilius, the source of Emilio.

e.meaning: farmer, one who works the earth
e.etymology: The Italian form of Georgia, the feminine of Giorgio (George), from Greek georgos, farmer: ge, earth, and ergon, work.
A respelling of Aviana, a modern name that reads as Ava joined to the -iana of Ariana and Liliana.
Mostly used as a spelling of Elian, a name connected with Elias and with the Roman name Aelianus. Sir Elyan the White is also a knight of Arthurian legend.
A recent American coinage that adds the -lynn ending to Scott, a surname for a Scot; a sister to Scottie and Scotlyn.

e.meaning: blend of Lee and Ann: meadow and grace
e.etymology: A blend of Lee and Ann, also written Leanne and LeAnn. Lee is Old English for a meadow or clearing, and Ann comes from Hebrew Hannah, grace.

e.meaning: from a Roman family name linked to Latin helvus, honey-yellow
e.etymology: The Spanish and Italian form of Helvia, the feminine of the Roman family name Helvius, linked to Latin helvus, honey-yellow. Most US bearers are from Mexican American families.

e.meaning: pet form of Barbara, foreign woman
e.etymology: A pet form of Barbara, from Greek barbaros, foreign. Mattel's doll, launched in 1959, was named for Barbara Handler, the daughter of its creator Ruth Handler.

assoc.t: Barbie, the 2023 hit film with Margot Robbie

e.note: Inseparable from the Mattel doll; Barbie is also used as a jab at a woman seen as pretty but shallow.

e.etymology: An English surname and place name, usually explained as land attached to a court or manor. It overlaps with Cortland, the spelling of several American towns.
From the Roman name Florianus, from Florus and Latin flos, flower. Saint Florian, a Roman soldier martyred in 304, is the patron of firefighters and of Upper Austria.

e.meaning: pet form of Veronica or Ronald
e.etymology: A spelling of Ronnie, the pet form of Veronica for girls and Ronald for boys. Ronald is from Old Norse Rognvaldr, ruler's counsel.
